title: Why retries can make a slow service collapse
subtitle: Follow requests, queues, capacity, feedback, failure, and redesign through a distributed information service.

learner_steps.prompt: Which visible result could be caused by several hidden stages rather than one slow server?
Choose the service boundary. Where do requests, responses, queues, state, and control information cross it?
Predict what happens to delay and backlog as offered load approaches or exceeds service capacity.
Distinguish a simple capacity shortage from a retry feedback loop that amplifies the original slowdown.
Preserve critical public information under load while balancing freshness, accessibility, privacy, reliability, and operational complexity.

equations: dB/dt = lambda_offered - mu while backlog is positive

prediction.legend: Before running the model, predict the service response.
choices: Delay remains close to one service time.
Delay and backlog grow sharply near or above capacity.

chart.title: Predicted queue response
chart.description_template: Backlog and delay under the selected arrival, capacity, retry, queue, and duration assumptions.

limitations: The model treats rates as averages and does not simulate burst distributions or several dependent queues.
The M/M/1 mean-delay relation is shown only when offered load is below capacity and its assumptions remain explicit.
Synthetic results do not predict a specific website, API, network, or school service.

diagnosis_challenge.question: A dependency slows, clients time out together, retries increase offered load, and the queue keeps growing after some capacity returns. What is the best first diagnosis?
options: The service only needs an unlimited queue so no request is rejected.
A retry feedback loop is amplifying the slowdown; retry ownership, backoff, deadlines, and queue bounds must be examined.
Low average utilization proves that the user-facing service is healthy.
The original operations definitely failed because clients timed out.
diagnosis_challenge.explanation: A timeout does not prove the original work stopped. Synchronized retries can increase offered load above degraded capacity, extend queues, and create a positive-feedback collapse.

requirements: Use fictional content and synthetic requests only.
Do not interact with a real website, API, school system, account, network, or device.
Keep all model execution local, bounded, and dependency-free.

atlas.decision: Defer Atlas expansion until implementation reveals a concrete exact-revision evidence gap.

reusable_shell_requirements: All model labels, controls, prediction choices, output names, chart semantics, and limitations must come from the route payload or a model adapter.
The learner shell must call a model adapter through validate, run, summarize, and describe-chart operations.
The generic challenge, evidence, navigation, notes, validation recovery, and accessibility contracts must remain route-independent.
Route-specific equations and calculations must not be embedded directly in the generic shell.
The refrigerator route must remain the default and retain deterministic output after distributed-information becomes independently runnable.
acceptance_criteria: A buildable software/product_alpha/routes/distributed-information.json exists only after the queue adapter is implemented.
Both refrigerator and distributed-information pass deterministic build checks.
The selected route renders five steps from canonical sources.
Prediction is required before the queue model runs.
Diagnosis is required before feedback is shown.
No live traffic, external dependency, persistence, analytics, account, or repository mutation is introduced.
Focused JavaScript and Python tests cover both model adapters and preserve refrigerator behavior.

may_claim: a buildable and loopback-runnable distributed-information local alpha route
a reusable learner shell demonstrated across thermal and queue model adapters
deterministic dual-route packaging with refrigerator preserved as default
does_not_establish: performance of a real distributed service
security of a real school system
